title: One Dataset's Shape, Two Datasets Compared

steps.body: A dot plot puts every value where it belongs on a number line, one dot per data point, stacked when values repeat. Nothing is summarized away yet — the whole dataset is right there, which is exactly why its **shape** is visible: where it peaks, whether it leans, and whether one value sits far from the rest.
Build the plot: 1 student scored 2, 1 scored 6, 2 scored 7, 3 scored 8, 3 scored 9.

predict.prompt: Ten quiz scores are mostly 7-9, but one student scored just 2. Will the dot plot look roughly symmetric, or will it lean?

options.label: Roughly symmetric — one low score won't shift the overall shape much
It will lean — a stretched tail toward the low outlier

predict.reveal: It leans. A cluster of high scores plus one far-off low score pulls a long tail toward 2 — watch that tail appear as you build it.

widget.prompt: Build the dot plot for the ten quiz scores.
widget.successFeedback: Ten dots, peaked at 8-9 with a long low tail reaching to 2. That tail is the outlier's fingerprint — nothing about the peak changed, but the shape is no longer symmetric.
widget.partialFeedback: Some stacks don't match yet. Recount from the data: 1 at 2, 1 at 6, 2 at 7, 3 at 8, 3 at 9.

steps.body: Read a count straight off the plot.
explanationVariants: The stack above 8 has 3 dots — 3 students scored an 8.
Count the dots directly above the value asked for.

widget.prompt: On this plot, how many students scored an 8?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 is the total of the three tallest stacks combined (2+3+3+1... not quite — read only the ONE stack above 8, not several).
1 is the height of the stack above 6, not 8.

steps.body: See what the outlier does to the range.
explanationVariants: 9 (highest) minus 2 (the outlier) is 7 — a big range driven by one point.
Range only needs the two extreme values, however many points sit between them.

widget.prompt: What is the range of all ten scores, INCLUDING the outlier at 2?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is 9 − 6, skipping the outlier entirely. The outlier IS one of the ten scores — include it.
2 is the outlier's value itself, not the range. Range is highest minus lowest: 9 − 2.

steps.body: Shape and range describe ONE dataset. Comparing TWO datasets needs the same two questions asked side by side: which is centred higher (or lower), and which is more spread out. A class that averages higher AND stays more consistent is doing better on both counts — a class that averages higher but swings wildly might not be, once you look past the average.
Build Class A's five-number summary: min 78, Q1 82, median 85, Q3 88, max 92.

widget.prompt: Set Class A's summary: min 78, Q1 82, median 85, Q3 88, max 92.
widget.successFeedback: That box is narrow — Q1 to Q3 spans only 6 points, all packed close to the median. A tight box IS the picture of consistency.
widget.orderFeedback: Keep the five handles in order: min ≤ Q1 ≤ median ≤ Q3 ≤ max.

steps.body: Compute the spread the box just showed.
explanationVariants: Q3 minus Q1 is 88 − 82 = 6 — the width of the box, the middle half of the class.
The IQR is exactly the box's width: Q3 − Q1.

widget.prompt: What is Class A's interquartile range (Q3 − Q1)?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 is max − min (92 − 78), the FULL range, not the box's width.
3 is half of 6. The IQR is the box's full width, Q3 minus Q1 directly.

explanationVariants: Class B's box would be much wider than Class A's — same median, but scores land anywhere from 70 to 100 instead of clustering near 85.
A wide range with the same average means less consistency, not more opportunity.
hints: Both classes average 85 — the medians would be about the same.
Class B's scores span 70 to 100. What does that say about its box's WIDTH compared to Class A's?
A wider box means MORE spread, which means LESS consistency.

widget.prompt: Class B has the same median as Class A but scores ranging from 70 to 100. What would Class B's box plot look like next to Class A's?

options.label: About the same centre, but a much wider box — less consistent
options.feedback: Same median, but a wide range of raw scores means a wide IQR too: Class B is far less consistent than Class A's tight cluster.

options.label: A much higher centre, similar width
options.feedback: The medians are given as roughly equal — the centres would match, not differ.

options.label: About the same centre and a narrower box
options.feedback: A WIDER range of raw scores (70-100 vs Class A's tighter cluster) means a WIDER box, not narrower.

options.label: There is no way to compare them without more data
options.feedback: The median and range given are exactly what a box plot needs — that IS enough to compare.

steps.body: One dataset's shape, and two datasets compared.
takeaways: A dot plot shows shape directly: peaks, symmetry, and how far an outlier's tail stretches.
Comparing groups needs both centre (median) and spread (IQR) — a higher average alone doesn't mean more consistent.
A narrow box is a tight cluster; a wide box is real variation, whatever the median says.
steps.teaser: next chapter: two-variable data — fitting a line, and reading what it says.

concept.body: Rewind. Range is the distance from the SMALLEST value to the LARGEST — highest minus lowest, nothing more. IQR is the same idea but for just the middle half: Q3 minus Q1.

explanationVariants: Range only needs the two extreme values.

widget.prompt: A dataset's smallest value is 5 and largest is 20. What is the range?

commonErrors.feedback: 25 adds them. Range SUBTRACTS: highest minus lowest.
4 divides them. Range is highest minus lowest: 20 − 5 = 15.
